title: Everything belongs to God, so the owners are stewards
setting: The United Firm was formed in 1832 to run the Church’s stores and printing. By 1834 it was deep in debt, and the Missouri store and press had been lost to mob violence. Some members were accused of treating firm property as their own. On 10 April 1834 the Kirtland members voted to dissolve the firm. This revelation, given at or near Kirtland on 23 April, instead reorganized it. The 1835 edition later used substitute names and called it the “United Order.”
summary: The revelation addresses the order the Lord commanded to be organized. It says some members broke the covenant through covetousness and feigned words, and are cursed. Members are to be organized and each given a stewardship to account for. It says the earth is the Lord’s, there is enough and to spare, and the poor are to be exalted. It assigns Kirtland properties to Sidney Rigdon, Martin Harris, Frederick Williams, Oliver Cowdery, John Johnson, Newel Whitney, and Joseph Smith. The Kirtland and Missouri branches are separated. Two treasuries are created, one for the sacred writings and one for stewardship income. Members are to pay their debts and write to New York, and may pledge their properties this once.

contextNote.title: Stewards, not owners
contextNote.text: The firm’s members had begun to treat shared property as their own. Verse 56 answers with a plain test: if the properties are the Lord’s, then the holders are stewards. Verse 55 states the premise that all these properties belong to the Lord. Verse 14 gives the reason, since the Lord made the earth and all things in it. Verse 70 applies this to money, which no one may call his own. In this passage, a steward holds and uses property but must account for it.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 102–105 teaches from this revelation that we are stewards over what God has given us. What do verses 13–18 say about who owns the earth and how its abundance should reach the poor?
reviewNote: Read all 86 verses. Official heading gives at or near Kirtland, 23 April 1834, to members of the United Firm, after the 10 April vote to dissolve. JSP historical introduction read for the firm’s debts, the loss of the Missouri store and press, the covetousness charges, the two treasuries, and the 1835 pseudonyms. Verse 81 says only “New York”; mapped to new-york-city because the firm’s creditors were New York suppliers. JSP says there is no evidence the treasuries were set up. Fact-check 2026-10-12: no changes. Setting checked against the official heading and JSP historical introduction.
